title: Abraham and the instinct to develop
stake: Whether the existence of a drive to develop shows that following it benefits everyone.
analyzedBy: claude-in-chat (pilot; corrected after a second-reader review)

asSaid.speaker: JORDAN PETERSON
asSaid.quote: Imagine that we have an instinct in us, or divine voice, I don’t care which of those you use, an instinct within us that calls us to develop

asSaid.speaker: JORDAN PETERSON
asSaid.quote: If you did that, to follow that instinct, then you’d be a blessing to yourself. Your name would become known among your people. You’d establish something of permanent significance. No one could stand before you, and it would bring abundance to everyone

asSaid.speaker: JORDAN PETERSON
asSaid.quote: that speaks of a concordance which has to be there

asSaid.speaker: JORDAN PETERSON
asSaid.quote: The alternative is preposterous, right? The alternative is that we don’t have an instinct to develop.

deflated.hs: Humans have a drive to grow and explore; you can see it in children. The Abraham story promises that following that drive brings five rewards: fulfillment, a good name, lasting work, no enemies left standing, and abundance for all. Peterson: since we obviously have the drive, the promise must hold, because the only alternative is that the drive does not exist, which is absurd.
deflated.g5: People are born curious and want to grow. The Bible story about Abraham says if you follow that urge, five great things happen to you and to everyone around you. Peterson says this must be true, because the only other option is that people aren't curious, and that's silly.

notes.hs: The rewrite condenses his five promises; 'no one could stand before you' is kept because it is the strongest. 'Preposterous' and 'stupid theory' are his words about the alternative.
notes.g5: The five promises were shortened. 'Preposterous' is his word.

jump.pivot: The alternative is preposterous, right? The alternative is that we don’t have an instinct to develop.
jump.hs: A false dichotomy. The alternative to 'following your drive brings abundance to everyone' is not 'the drive does not exist'. It is 'the drive exists and often leads to ruin, or to your gain at others' cost', which is also visible in children and in history. The five-part promise is asserted; the only thing argued is the existence of curiosity, which nobody disputes.
jump.g5: He says it's either 'follow your drive and everything goes well' or 'there's no drive'. But there's a third option: the drive is real and sometimes leads you off a cliff, or you win while others lose. He proves people are curious, which nobody argued about, and skips the five promises.

defense.hs: Peterson does name a second alternative a few lines later: that what brings you into the world is 'done at the expense of other people', the power orientation, and he argues against it on the ground that it does not iterate socially. So the dichotomy is not as bare as the pivot line suggests. The concordance claim is framed as an evolutionary conjecture put to a biologist, not as a proof.
defense.g5: A little later he does mention another option: getting ahead by hurting others. He argues that doesn't last. So he isn't only giving two choices. And he says this is an idea he tested on a scientist friend, not a proven fact.

revision.hs: The challenge narrows: he considers two alternatives, not one, and dismisses the second with an argument ('it doesn't iterate'). What remains unargued is the leap from 'development instinct exists and power fails' to 'development brings abundance to everyone'; benign failure (the drive leads somewhere harmless but useless) is never considered. Citing Bret Weinstein's change of mind is an appeal to a convert, not evidence, and that stands.
revision.g5: He gives two other options, not one, and argues against the second. But he never considers that following your drive might just not work out. And a friend changing his mind isn't proof.

claims.text: Genesis 12 promises Abraham blessing, a name, permanence, victory over enemies, and abundance for all.
claims.speaker: JORDAN PETERSON

basis.hs: A fair paraphrase of the covenant promises.
basis.g5: Yes, that's roughly what the story says.

claims.text: Following the development instinct brings those five outcomes.
claims.speaker: JORDAN PETERSON

basis.hs: Asserted, defended by ruling out alternatives, never shown.
basis.g5: He says it but doesn't show it.

claims.text: There must be a concordance between what develops us and what benefits the world.
claims.speaker: JORDAN PETERSON

basis.hs: An evolutionary conjecture; the opposite (traits good for the individual, bad for the group) is common in biology.
basis.g5: A guess about evolution. In nature, what's good for one animal is often bad for the group.
